modules.title: JSON and JSONB
modules.goal: Store, query, index and update semi-structured data without losing relational discipline.

topics.title: JSON vs JSONB
topics.simple: JSON text hai; JSONB parsed binary hai.
topics.pro: JSON stores the original text, while JSONB parses it into a binary form that supports indexing and efficient operators.
points: JSONB is usually the better default.
JSONB loses key order and duplicates.

example.sql: SELECT '{"name":"Aarav"}'::jsonb AS data;

topics.title: JSON Literals
topics.simple: JSON literal quoted object ya array hota hai.
topics.pro: A JSON literal is cast with ::json or ::jsonb and can contain objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null.
points: Use single quotes around the literal.
JSON null is not SQL NULL.

example.sql: SELECT '{"name":"Aarav","marks":90}'::jsonb AS student;

topics.title: Storing JSONB
topics.simple: JSONB column semi-structured data ke liye hota hai.
topics.pro: A jsonb column stores flexible attributes while the table keeps relational keys and constraints.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE events (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, payload JSONB NOT NULL);

topics.title: Arrow Operator
topics.simple: -> JSON value ko JSON ke roop me nikaalta hai.
topics.pro: The -> operator returns a JSONB value, preserving quotes and structure for chaining.
points: Works with object keys and array indexes.

example.sql: SELECT payload->'name' AS name_json FROM events;

topics.title: Text Arrow Operator
topics.simple: ->> JSON value ko text me nikaalta hai.
topics.pro: The ->> operator returns text, which is what you usually want for comparisons and display.
points: Casts numbers and booleans to text.
Use it in WHERE and ORDER BY.

example.sql: SELECT payload->>'name' AS name FROM events;

topics.title: Path Operators
topics.simple: #> and #>> nested paths nikaalte hain.
topics.pro: #> returns a JSONB value at a path array and #>> returns text at that path.
points: The path is a text array.

example.sql: SELECT payload#>'{address,city}' AS city_json, payload#>>'{address,city}' AS city FROM events;
example.output: The nested city value and text.

topics.title: JSONB Operators
topics.simple: JSONB mein containment, existence aur deletion operators hote hain.
topics.pro: JSONB supports @>, ?, ?|, ?&, ||, -, #- and path operators for querying and editing documents.

example.sql: SELECT payload || '{"active":true}'::jsonb AS merged FROM events;

topics.title: Containment
topics.simple: @> check karta hai ki JSONB doosre ko contain karta hai.
topics.pro: The @> operator tests whether the left JSONB contains the right structure, including nested keys and array elements.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM events WHERE payload @> '{"active":true}'::jsonb;

topics.title: Key Existence
topics.simple: ? operator key ya array element ki existence check karta hai.
topics.pro: The ? operator tests whether a top-level key or array string exists; ?| and ?& test any or all keys.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM events WHERE payload ? 'email';

topics.title: jsonb_each
topics.simple: jsonb_each object ko key/value rows me todta hai.
topics.pro: jsonb_each expands a top-level object into rows, enabling relational processing of dynamic keys.
points: Use it in a lateral join.

example.sql: SELECT key, value FROM events, LATERAL jsonb_each(payload);

topics.title: jsonb_array_elements
topics.simple: jsonb_array_elements array ko rows me todta hai.
topics.pro: jsonb_array_elements expands a JSON array into one row per element, which is useful for tags and line items.

example.sql: SELECT value FROM events, LATERAL jsonb_array_elements(payload->'tags');

topics.title: Building JSON
topics.simple: jsonb_build_object aur jsonb_build_array JSON banate hain.
topics.pro: jsonb_build_object and jsonb_build_array construct JSONB from SQL values, and jsonb_agg aggregates rows into an array.

example.sql: SELECT jsonb_build_object('name', name, 'marks', marks) AS student FROM students;

topics.title: Updating JSONB
topics.simple: jsonb_set nested value update karta hai.
topics.pro: jsonb_set replaces a value at a path, with an optional create_missing flag.
points: The path is a text array.
Missing paths are left alone unless create_missing is true.

example.sql: UPDATE events SET payload = jsonb_set(payload, '{active}', 'true'::jsonb) WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Deleting Keys
topics.simple: Minus operator key ya array element hataata hai.
topics.pro: The - operator removes a top-level key or array element, while #- removes a nested path.

example.sql: UPDATE events SET payload = payload - 'email' WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: JSON Path
topics.simple: jsonb_path_query JSONPath expressions chalata hai.
topics.pro: jsonb_path_query evaluates a SQL/JSON path and returns matching values, supporting filters and recursive descent.

example.sql: SELECT jsonb_path_query(payload, '$.tags[*]') FROM events;

topics.title: Indexing JSONB
topics.simple: GIN index JSONB containment aur existence ko fast karta hai.
topics.pro: A GIN index on a jsonb column accelerates @>, ?, ?| and ?& queries.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX idx_events_payload ON events USING gin (payload);

topics.title: JSON vs Relational
topics.simple: Stable fields columns me rakho; flexible fields JSONB me.
topics.pro: Relational columns give typed constraints and joins, while JSONB gives flexibility for sparse or evolving attributes.
points: Do not hide core keys in JSON.

example.sql: CREATE TABLE events (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, kind TEXT NOT NULL, payload JSONB NOT NULL);

topics.title: Validation
topics.simple: JSONB type aur shape ko CHECK se validate karo.
topics.pro: A CHECK constraint can require an object or a specific key, but deep schema validation often belongs in the application or a JSON schema validator.

example.sql: ALTER TABLE events ADD CONSTRAINT payload_object CHECK (jsonb_typeof(payload) = 'object');

topics.title: Common JSON Errors
topics.simple: Missing casts, wrong arrows aur array assumptions common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are comparing jsonb to text, using -> when ->> is needed, and calling array functions on a non-array.

example.sql: SELECT payload->>'name' FROM events WHERE payload->>'active' = 'true';

topics.title: Practical API Data
topics.simple: JSONB ko API payload, audit metadata aur flexible settings ke liye use karo.
topics.pro: A practical JSONB design keeps identity and relationships relational and stores the flexible payload with a GIN index for the queries that matter.

example.sql:
CREATE TABLE api_events (id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, kind TEXT NOT NULL, payload JSONB NOT NULL, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW());
CREATE INDEX api_events_payload_gin ON api_events USING gin (payload);

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain JSON vs JSONB in a production query.
interview.answer: JSON stores the original text, while JSONB parses it into a binary form that supports indexing and efficient operators. Key rules: JSON preserves formatting. JSONB is usually the better default. JSONB loses key order and duplicates.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain JSON Literals in a production query.
interview.answer: A JSON literal is cast with ::json or ::jsonb and can contain objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. Key rules: Use single quotes around the literal. Cast to jsonb. JSON null is not SQL NULL.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Storing JSONB in a production query.
interview.answer: A jsonb column stores flexible attributes while the table keeps relational keys and constraints. Key rules: Use jsonb for queryable documents. Keep stable fields as columns. Add a CHECK for jsonb_typeof.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Arrow Operator in a production query.
interview.answer: The -> operator returns a JSONB value, preserving quotes and structure for chaining. Key rules: Returns jsonb. Works with object keys and array indexes. Chain it for nested values.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Text Arrow Operator in a production query.
interview.answer: The ->> operator returns text, which is what you usually want for comparisons and display. Key rules: Returns text. Casts numbers and booleans to text. Use it in WHERE and ORDER BY.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Path Operators in a production query.
interview.answer: #> returns a JSONB value at a path array and #>> returns text at that path. Key rules: The path is a text array. Use braces in a literal. Chain arrows for simple paths.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain JSONB Operators in a production query.
interview.answer: JSONB supports @>, ?, ?|, ?&, ||, -, #- and path operators for querying and editing documents. Key rules: @> tests containment. ? tests key existence. || merges objects.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Containment in a production query.
interview.answer: The @> operator tests whether the left JSONB contains the right structure, including nested keys and array elements. Key rules: It is indexable with GIN. Objects match by key/value. Arrays match elements.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Key Existence in a production query.
interview.answer: The ? operator tests whether a top-level key or array string exists; ?| and ?& test any or all keys. Key rules: ? tests one key. ?| tests any key. ?& tests all keys.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain jsonb_each in a production query.
interview.answer: jsonb_each expands a top-level object into rows, enabling relational processing of dynamic keys. Key rules: It returns key and value. jsonb_each_text returns text. Use it in a lateral join.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain jsonb_array_elements in a production query.
interview.answer: jsonb_array_elements expands a JSON array into one row per element, which is useful for tags and line items. Key rules: It requires an array. Use WITH ORDINALITY for positions. It can multiply rows.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Building JSON in a production query.
interview.answer: jsonb_build_object and jsonb_build_array construct JSONB from SQL values, and jsonb_agg aggregates rows into an array. Key rules: Build objects from key/value pairs. Build arrays from values. Aggregate rows with jsonb_agg.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Updating JSONB in a production query.
interview.answer: jsonb_set replaces a value at a path, with an optional create_missing flag. Key rules: The path is a text array. The new value is JSONB. Missing paths are left alone unless create_missing is true.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Deleting Keys in a production query.
interview.answer: The - operator removes a top-level key or array element, while #- removes a nested path. Key rules: - removes a key. - integer removes an array element. #- removes a path.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain JSON Path in a production query.
interview.answer: jsonb_path_query evaluates a SQL/JSON path and returns matching values, supporting filters and recursive descent. Key rules: Paths start with $. It can return multiple rows. It supports filter expressions.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Indexing JSONB in a production query.
interview.answer: A GIN index on a jsonb column accelerates @>, ?, ?| and ?& queries. Key rules: Use gin (column). jsonb_ops is the default. jsonb_path_ops is smaller for containment.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain JSON vs Relational in a production query.
interview.answer: Relational columns give typed constraints and joins, while JSONB gives flexibility for sparse or evolving attributes. Key rules: Do not hide core keys in JSON. Use JSONB for optional metadata. Index the paths you query.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Validation in a production query.
interview.answer: A CHECK constraint can require an object or a specific key, but deep schema validation often belongs in the application or a JSON schema validator. Key rules: Use jsonb_typeof. Check required keys. Do not overconstrain flexible payloads.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Common JSON Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are comparing jsonb to text, using -> when ->> is needed, and calling array functions on a non-array. Key rules: Cast literals to jsonb. Use ->> for text. Check jsonb_typeof before array expansion.

interview.q: Module 22 · Explain Practical API Data in a production query.
interview.answer: A practical JSONB design keeps identity and relationships relational and stores the flexible payload with a GIN index for the queries that matter. Key rules: Keep keys relational. Store the payload. Index searched paths. Validate the top level.

logic.answer: JSONB supports @>, ?, ?|, ?&, ||, -, #- and path operators for querying and editing documents. @> tests containment. ? tests key existence. || merges objects.
The @> operator tests whether the left JSONB contains the right structure, including nested keys and array elements. It is indexable with GIN. Objects match by key/value. Arrays match elements.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does Key Existence matter?
logic.answer: The ? operator tests whether a top-level key or array string exists; ?| and ?& test any or all keys. ? tests one key. ?| tests any key. ?& tests all keys.
jsonb_each expands a top-level object into rows, enabling relational processing of dynamic keys. It returns key and value. jsonb_each_text returns text. Use it in a lateral join.
jsonb_array_elements expands a JSON array into one row per element, which is useful for tags and line items. It requires an array. Use WITH ORDINALITY for positions. It can multiply rows.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does Building JSON matter?
logic.answer: jsonb_build_object and jsonb_build_array construct JSONB from SQL values, and jsonb_agg aggregates rows into an array. Build objects from key/value pairs. Build arrays from values. Aggregate rows with jsonb_agg.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does Updating JSONB matter?
logic.answer: jsonb_set replaces a value at a path, with an optional create_missing flag. The path is a text array. The new value is JSONB. Missing paths are left alone unless create_missing is true.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does Deleting Keys matter?
logic.answer: The - operator removes a top-level key or array element, while #- removes a nested path. - removes a key. - integer removes an array element. #- removes a path.

logic.q: Module 22 · Why does JSON Path matter?
logic.answer: jsonb_path_query evaluates a SQL/JSON path and returns matching values, supporting filters and recursive descent. Paths start with $. It can return multiple rows. It supports filter expressions.
